title: The Internet, the Web, Browsers and Modern Web Applications
learningObjectives: Distinguish the internet's interconnected network infrastructure from the World Wide Web as one service that operates over it.
Explain the roles of clients, servers, routers, DNS resolvers, URLs and web browsers in a typical page request.
Describe at a high level how a browser resolves a domain, establishes a transport connection, negotiates secure communication and requests a resource.
Differentiate a website, a web page and a web application using their structure, behaviour and user tasks while recognizing that the categories overlap.
Explain the responsibilities of HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser's document, presentation and interaction layers.
Interpret the main components of a URL, including scheme, host, optional port, path, query and fragment.
Explain the purpose of HTTP methods, response status codes and headers at a conceptual level.
Distinguish HTTP from HTTPS and explain the role of TLS without assuming encryption guarantees trustworthy content.
Identify how browser caches, service workers, content delivery networks and redirects can affect a navigation.
Explain the concepts of origin and browser security boundaries at a beginner level, including why a page cannot freely read every other site's data.
Distinguish client-side interface responsibilities from server-side data storage, authentication, authorization and business rules.
Trace a simplified request-response lifecycle and identify where common network, server, resource-loading and runtime failures can occur.

understand.concept: The internet is a global system of interconnected networks that exchange data using agreed protocols. The World Wide Web is an information system built on top of that infrastructure: resources are identified by URLs, transferred using web protocols such as HTTP, and interpreted by software such as browsers. The Web is not the internet itself; email, file transfer, voice communication and many other services can also use the internet. A browser is a client application that requests resources, processes documents and provides a runtime for web technologies. A modern web application combines browser-side code with server-side services and data.
understand.whyItMatters: Front-end development becomes much easier to reason about when you know which part of the system is responsible for a behaviour. A browser cannot fix a DNS failure by changing CSS; a server response problem is not the same as a JavaScript exception; and a URL is an identifier, not the page itself. The same understanding helps you recognize where security decisions belong: the browser can improve the user experience, but the server must protect data and authorize sensitive operations.
understand.history: The internet's packet-switched networking foundations predate the Web. Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989; the first website and browser followed in the early 1990s. The Web combined hypertext, resource identifiers and network protocols into a practical system for sharing linked information. As browsers gained scripting and richer APIs, websites evolved into interactive applications while retaining the core client/server and resource-addressing model.
understand.analogy: A useful model is to treat the internet as the underlying delivery infrastructure and the Web as one service that uses it to deliver linked resources.
understand.analogyLimit: This comparison is not a literal map of the internet. Web resources can be cached, dynamically generated, distributed across many servers, or delivered through content networks; a browser also parses and executes code after receiving data.

explain.narrative:
A browser acts as a client. When a user enters a URL, the browser parses the address and identifies the destination host. It may use a cached DNS answer or ask a configured resolver to discover address information. It then establishes an appropriate transport connection. For HTTPS, TLS protects communication in transit; HTTP defines the request and response semantics. The browser sends a request, commonly using a method such as GET, and the server or an intermediary returns a response with a status code, headers and often a body.

The browser then processes the returned resources. HTML is parsed into a document structure, CSS contributes styling and layout, and JavaScript can execute to add behaviour or update the page. A single document may cause many additional requests for stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts and API data. Redirects, caches, service workers and content delivery networks can change where a response comes from and how many network operations are required.

A website is a related collection of pages and resources. A web page is one document or view. A web application provides interactive tasks such as editing a document, filtering records, submitting a workflow or managing an account. These labels overlap: a website may contain application features, and an application may contain informational pages. Classify the experience by what users do, not only by how it looks.

Most applications divide responsibilities between the client and server. The browser renders the interface, collects input and may perform immediate validation. A server stores protected data, applies business rules, authenticates callers and authorizes operations. Browser code is delivered to the user's device and can be inspected or modified; hiding a button or checking a field in JavaScript does not secure a protected operation.

The browser also enforces security boundaries. An origin is based on the scheme, host and port, and browser rules restrict how one origin can access data belonging to another. These protections help prevent one site from freely reading another site's private data. They do not replace server authorization or safe application design.

Real navigation is more complex than one request. A browser may reuse a connection, follow redirects, use cached resources, request multiple assets in parallel and execute scripts that make later API calls. When a problem occurs, identify the layer: DNS, connection, TLS, HTTP response, resource URL, HTML parsing, CSS calculation, JavaScript runtime or server-side processing.

examples.title: A simplified request-response lifecycle
examples.code:
Browser
  │  GET /guide HTTP request
  ▼
Web server
  │  200 OK + response body
  ▼
Browser parses HTML, loads CSS/JS and renders the page
examples.explanation: This is a conceptual sequence, not a complete network trace. A real page can trigger many additional requests for stylesheets, scripts, images, fonts and API data.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser displays the requested resource if the request and subsequent processing succeed.

examples.title: Read the parts of a URL
examples.code:
https://learn.example.org:443/courses/html?level=advanced#forms

scheme:   https
host:     learn.example.org
port:     443
path:     /courses/html
query:    ?level=advanced
fragment: #forms
examples.explanation: The scheme indicates the access protocol, the host identifies the destination, the path selects a resource, the query carries parameters, and the fragment identifies a location or state within the resource. The default HTTPS port is normally omitted from visible URLs.
examples.expectedOutput: You can identify the destination and the resource path without confusing the URL with the page's content.

examples.title: Website and web application are overlapping terms
examples.code:
Information site: read an article, follow links, view references
Web application: sign in, edit a document, filter records, submit a workflow
examples.explanation: A website may contain interactive application features, and an application may contain informational pages. The distinction is about the primary user tasks, not a strict technical boundary.
examples.expectedOutput: You can explain the purpose of the experience rather than classify it only by appearance.

examples.title: Client, server and supporting services
examples.code:
Browser client
  ├─ parses the URL
  ├─ requests resources
  ├─ processes HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  └─ displays the interface

Supporting systems
  ├─ DNS resolver: helps find address information
  ├─ network: carries packets between endpoints
  ├─ CDN/cache: may serve a stored response
  └─ application server: handles requests and business rules
examples.explanation: A browser navigation can involve several independent systems. DNS does not render the page, a CDN does not necessarily run the application's business logic, and the browser is responsible for processing the returned web resources.
examples.expectedOutput: You can name the major components and explain their responsibilities.

examples.title: A request and response communicate intent and outcome
examples.code:
GET /courses/html HTTP/1.1
Host: learn.example.test
Accept: text/html

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Cache-Control: max-age=60
examples.explanation: The request method expresses the kind of operation, the target identifies the resource, and headers provide metadata. The response status describes the outcome and response headers describe the returned representation and caching rules. Modern HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use different wire framing while retaining HTTP semantics.
examples.expectedOutput: You can identify a method, target, status and headers in a simplified HTTP exchange.

examples.title: HTTP and HTTPS have different transport protection
examples.code:
HTTP:
- HTTP request/response semantics
- no TLS protection by default

HTTPS:
- HTTP semantics carried over a TLS-protected connection
- helps protect confidentiality and integrity in transit
- authenticates the server's certificate for the hostname
examples.explanation: HTTPS helps protect data while it travels between the client and server. It does not prove that a website's content is honest, safe or free of malicious behaviour.
examples.expectedOutput: You can explain what HTTPS protects and what it does not guarantee.

examples.title: The browser applies origin-based security boundaries
examples.code:
Origin = scheme + host + port

https://shop.example.test:443
https://shop.example.test:8443
http://shop.example.test:80

These are different origins because the scheme or port differs.
examples.explanation: The same-origin policy restricts how a document or script from one origin can access certain data from another origin. Cross-origin communication is possible through controlled mechanisms such as CORS and postMessage, but it is not unrestricted.
examples.expectedOutput: You can identify when two example URLs have different origins.

practise.guidedTask: For a page that loads a product catalogue, write down the client, the server, the URL host, the requested path, one likely HTML resource, one CSS resource and one JavaScript resource. Then explain what happens if DNS resolution fails, if the server returns 503, and if the HTML loads but one stylesheet returns 404. Identify which system or browser tool provides evidence for each failure.
practise.independentTask: Use your browser's Developer Tools on a public page. Inspect the Network panel and identify the document request, at least one stylesheet, one script, response status codes, caching information and any redirects. Describe which parts run in the browser and which likely run on the server. Record observations without copying private tokens, cookies, authorization headers or personal data.
hints: DNS translates a host name into address information; it does not render a page.
HTTP defines request and response semantics. HTTPS protects the connection using TLS; it does not guarantee that a website's content is trustworthy.
A browser is both a user interface and a complex client runtime: it parses documents, applies styles, executes scripts and enforces security boundaries.
A web page is one resource or document. A website is a related collection of resources. A web application provides interactive tasks; these categories can overlap.
Use the Network panel to inspect requests and the Console to inspect JavaScript messages. They answer different debugging questions.
HTTPS protects communication in transit but does not prove that the website or its content is trustworthy.
The browser's same-origin policy limits cross-origin access; CORS and other explicit mechanisms control selected cross-origin interactions.
Authentication identifies a caller; authorization determines what that caller may do. Protected operations must be enforced by the server.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes the relationship between the internet and the Web most accurately?
options: The Web is the physical network that connects all devices.
The Web is an information system that uses the internet; other internet services exist too.
The internet is a feature provided by web browsers.
questions.answer: The Web is an information system that uses the internet; other internet services exist too.
questions.explanation: The internet provides interconnected networking infrastructure. The Web is one service built on that infrastructure.

questions.prompt: At which point in a typical navigation is DNS most directly involved?
options: When the browser applies CSS selectors.
When a host name must be resolved to network address information.
When JavaScript updates an element's text.
questions.answer: When a host name must be resolved to network address information.
questions.explanation: DNS resolution helps the client discover where to send network traffic. It is separate from HTML parsing, CSS calculation and JavaScript execution.

questions.prompt: A request receives an HTTP 404 response. What does this primarily indicate?
options: The browser could not parse CSS.
The requested resource was not found at the requested location.
The user's JavaScript contains a syntax error.
questions.answer: The requested resource was not found at the requested location.
questions.explanation: A 404 is an HTTP response status associated with a missing resource. It is not a JavaScript or CSS parsing error.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best represents the browser's high-level work after receiving an HTML document?
options: Parse document structure, discover/load related resources, calculate styles and render; execute scripts according to loading and runtime rules.
Convert every HTML element directly into a database table.
Run CSS first as a programming language, then ask the server to create HTML.
questions.answer: Parse document structure, discover/load related resources, calculate styles and render; execute scripts according to loading and runtime rules.
questions.explanation: Browser processing involves multiple coordinated stages and can include additional resource requests and script execution. The exact pipeline is more detailed than this overview.

questions.prompt: Which URL components determine an origin?
options: Scheme, host and port
Path, query and fragment
HTML tag, CSS class and JavaScript function
questions.explanation: The origin is defined by the scheme, host and port. The path, query and fragment do not form part of the origin.

questions.prompt: What does HTTPS primarily add to HTTP?
options: TLS protection for communication in transit
A guarantee that the website's content is trustworthy
Automatic server-side authorization for every action
questions.answer: TLS protection for communication in transit
questions.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection using TLS. It does not guarantee that content is safe or that application authorization is correct.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility must a server enforce for a protected account operation?
options: Authentication and authorization of the request
The colour of the browser button
The local page's CSS selector names
questions.answer: Authentication and authorization of the request
questions.explanation: Client-side checks can be modified or bypassed. The server must verify the caller and authorize each protected operation.
